definition: Bayesian programming is a formalism and a methodology for having a technique to specify probabilistic models and solve problems when less than the necessary information is available.
details: Edwin T. Jaynes proposed that probability could be considered as an alternative and an extension of logic for rational reasoning with incomplete and uncertain information. In his founding book Probability Theory: The Logic of Science he developed this theory and proposed what he called "the robot," which was not a physical device, but an inference engine to automate probabilistic reasoning—a kind of Prolog for probability instead of logic. Bayesian programming is a formal and concrete implementation of this "robot". Bayesian programming may also be seen as an algebraic formalism to specify graphical models such as, for instance, Bayesian networks, dynamic Bayesian networks, Kalman filters or hidden Markov models. Indeed, Bayesian programming is more general than Bayesian networks and has a power of expression equivalent to probabilistic factor graphs.

explainer.lead: Bayesian programming is a way to describe uncertain situations as probabilistic models and draw reasoned conclusions even when some information is missing. It turns Edwin T. Jaynes’s idea of probability as an extension of logic into a concrete method for automated inference.

tiers.eli5: Imagine trying to solve a puzzle with some pieces missing: you can still make a careful guess from the pieces you have. Bayesian programming gives a computer a way to describe how different clues relate, then work out how likely each possible answer is. It does not pretend to know the missing pieces for certain.
tiers.practitioner: Use Bayesian programming to specify a probabilistic model, provide the observations that are available, and perform inference over what remains unknown. It can express Bayesian networks, dynamic Bayesian networks, Kalman filters, and hidden Markov models, while offering greater generality than Bayesian networks alone. A key pitfall is treating its probabilistic output as certainty rather than reasoning conditioned on incomplete information.
tiers.paperLevel: Bayesian programming is a formalism and methodology for specifying probabilistic models and performing inference under incomplete information. It is a concrete implementation of the inference engine Jaynes called “the robot” in Probability Theory: The Logic of Science, based on probability as an extension of logic. It is more general than Bayesian networks and has expressive power equivalent to probabilistic factor graphs.

explainer.example: Suppose a model connects rain with the probability of wet grass. If you observe wet grass but have no direct observation of rain, Bayesian inference can estimate how likely rain is by using that relationship, rather than giving a definite yes-or-no answer from incomplete evidence.

usedIn.name: Bayesian networks
usedIn.detail: Can be specified using Bayesian programming as graphical probabilistic models.

usedIn.name: Dynamic Bayesian networks
usedIn.detail: Can be described within the same algebraic formalism.

usedIn.name: Kalman filters
usedIn.detail: One of the graphical-model forms Bayesian programming can specify.

usedIn.name: Hidden Markov models
usedIn.detail: Can be expressed alongside other probabilistic graphical models.

explainer.intuition: Logic works well when the needed facts are available, but many problems contain gaps and uncertainty. Bayesian programming uses probabilities to represent what is known and unknown, then infers reasoned answers instead of requiring complete information.
howItWorks: Describe the uncertain quantities in the problem.
Specify their probabilistic relationships as a model.
Provide the observations that are available.
Use inference to reason about the unobserved quantities.
Return probabilistic conclusions rather than unjustified certainties.
explainer.whyItMatters: It provides a general, concrete way to automate rational reasoning when information is incomplete or uncertain. Its expressive power covers several widely used graphical-model forms and matches that of probabilistic factor graphs.
misconceptions: It is not limited to Bayesian networks; it is more general.
Jaynes’s “robot” was an inference engine, not a physical device.
Probabilistic reasoning does not turn incomplete evidence into certainty.

diagram.caption: A Bayesian program combines a probabilistic model with available evidence to infer conclusions about unknown quantities.
